rounds.proof_sketch: The mutation is in `diag_matmul_kernel`. The dispatch condition is `if (M >= 1024)` → use optimized kernel, else use simple kernel (containing mutation). With fixed shape B=[4096, 4096], M=4096 >= 1024 is always TRUE. Therefore `diag_matmul_kernel_optimized` is always called, and `diag_matmul_kernel` (containing the mutation) is NEVER executed.
rounds.survival_reason: The mutant survives because the mutation exists in dead code for the given fixed input configuration. The CUDA code has two kernel implementations: `diag_matmul_kernel` (simple) and `diag_matmul_kernel_optimized`. The dispatch logic at line 51-53 selects the optimized kernel when M >= 1024. With the fixed input shape B=[4096, 4096], M=4096 which satisfies M >= 1024, so the optimized kernel is always selected. The mutation on line 20 modifying `col < M` to `col < M - 1` is in `diag_matmul_kernel`, which is never invoked. No value-level test can change which kernel is dispatched since dispatch depends solely on the shape parameter M, not on tensor values.
rounds.kill_strategy: Unkillable under fixed-shape contract. The mutation is in `diag_matmul_kernel` which is only called when M < 1024. With fixed M=4096, this kernel path is never executed. Only changing M to a value < 1024 would trigger the mutated path, which violates the fixed-shape contract.
rounds.recommendations: Mutation testing frameworks should track kernel dispatch paths and identify mutations in code paths that are unreachable given fixed input configurations. When a kernel has multiple implementations selected by dimension-based conditionals, mutations in unreachable implementations are inherently unkillable without configuration changes. Consider testing both kernel paths by having separate test configurations with appropriate shapes.
